# Exact optimal-depth bound for log-concave densities

This is an ordinary continuous auxiliary theorem. It does not assert that
a suitable log-concave target can be constructed from an arbitrary
mixed-integer set.

## Theorem

Let r>=1 and let f:R^r->[0,infinity) be a log-concave probability density
with full-dimensional support. For a point y define

    D_f(y)=inf{integral_H f: H is a closed halfspace containing y}.

Then the maximum is attained at a point of the interior of the support,
and

    max_y D_f(y) >= gamma_r=(r/(r+1))^r.

The constant is sharp, because a uniform probability density on an
r-dimensional simplex is log-concave and has maximum depth gamma_r.

The proof combines an explicit radial-integral convexity argument with
an optimality certificate. Crucially, the radial body is constructed
around a maximum-depth point, rather than an arbitrary mean or mode.

## Lemma 1: elementary bounds for an integrable log-concave density

After translating any interior point of {f>0} to zero, there exist
positive constants m,delta,A,c such that

    f(x)>=m for |x|<=delta,
    f(x)<=A exp(-c|x|) for every x.

Proof. The logarithm of f is a finite concave function on the interior
of its convex positive set, and is therefore continuous there. This
gives the first assertion. A global upper bound follows by applying
log-concavity at midpoints: for fixed x and every v in B(0,delta),

    f((x+v)/2)>=sqrt(f(x)m).

Integrating over that translated ball bounds f(x) by a constant
independent of x. The same argument excludes an infinite value of f.

The convex superlevel set E={f>=f(0)/2} contains a ball around zero and
must be bounded. Otherwise, its convex hull with that ball contains
cones of arbitrarily large volume, contradicting integrability of f.
Choose R with E subset {|x|<R}. For |x|>=R, log-concavity on [0,x] gives

    f(Rx/|x|)>=f(0)^(1-R/|x|) f(x)^(R/|x|).

The left side is less than f(0)/2. Rearranging proves an exponential
upper bound outside the ball; enlarge its multiplicative constant to
cover the ball using the already established global upper bound. QED.

## Lemma 2: convexity of the radial-integral body

Let f be as in Lemma 1 with zero an interior positive point, and let p>0.
For x!=0 put

    I_p(x)=integral_0^infinity t^(p-1) f(tx) dt,
    q_p(x)=I_p(x)^(-1/p),

and put q_p(0)=0. Then q_p is a finite continuous convex positively
homogeneous function. In particular its unit sublevel set is a convex
body containing zero in its interior.

Proof. The bounds in Lemma 1 give positive finite upper and lower bounds
for I_p on the unit sphere. Homogeneity follows by a change of variable:
I_p(cx)=c^(-p)I_p(x) for c>0.

We prove convexity of the unit sublevel set by considering two points
x,y with I_p(x)=I_p(y)=1. Fix 0<lambda<1 and z=lambda x+(1-lambda)y.
The case z=0 is immediate. Couple the two probability densities

    r^(p-1) f(rx) dr,  s^(p-1) f(sy) ds

by their increasing quantiles r(u),s(u), 0<u<1. On each ray the positive
set is an interval starting at zero, and f is positive and continuous
before its endpoint. Thus the quantiles are continuously differentiable
in (0,1), with

    r'=1/[r^(p-1)f(rx)],
    s'=1/[s^(p-1)f(sy)].

Define, for each u,

    t=(lambda/r+(1-lambda)/s)^(-1),
    a=lambda t/r, b=(1-lambda)t/s.

Then a,b>0, a+b=1, and

    tz=a rx+b sy,    t=ar+bs.

Log-concavity implies f(tz)>=f(rx)^a f(sy)^b. Differentiating t gives

    t'=t^2[lambda r'/r^2+(1-lambda)s'/s^2]>0.

Writing f_1=f(rx), f_2=f(sy), the last identities yield

    t^(p-1) f(tz)t'
      >= t^p f_1^a f_2^b [a/(r^p f_1)+b/(s^p f_2)]
      >= t^p/(r^(pa)s^(pb))
      >= 1.

The second inequality is weighted arithmetic-geometric mean applied to
1/(r^p f_1) and 1/(s^p f_2). The third uses t=ar+bs>=r^a s^b.

As u increases from zero to one, t increases from zero to some endpoint
T<=infinity. Changing variables and integrating the displayed inequality
gives

    I_p(z)>=integral_0^T t^(p-1)f(tz)dt>=integral_0^1 1 du=1.

Hence every segment between two boundary points remains in the unit
sublevel set. Positive homogeneity and inclusion of zero extend this to
all of its points: express a convex combination of two arbitrary points
as a combination of their radial boundary points and zero.

For completeness, I_p is continuous on the sphere. If directions
u_j->u, then f(tu_j)->f(tu) for almost every t>0: along the ray from an
interior point there is at most one boundary value, and otherwise tu is
either interior to the support or exterior to its closure. The uniform
exponential majorant in Lemma 1 permits dominated convergence. Thus the
radial unit sublevel set is closed, and the radial bounds make it compact
with a ball around zero. Its gauge q_p is continuous and convex. QED.

This is a direct proof of the needed form of Ball's radial-integral
convexity theorem. It does not require f(0) to be the maximum of f.

## Lemma 3: existence and active-normal certificate for a deepest point

There exists y in the interior of the support attaining alpha=max D_f.
Moreover there exist unit vectors u_1,...,u_m, with m<=r+1, and positive
weights lambda_i summing to one such that

    sum_i lambda_i u_i=0,
    integral_{u_i dot (x-y)>=0} f(x)dx=alpha for every i.

Proof. Every hyperplane has f-measure zero. Therefore

    G(y,u)=integral_{u dot (x-y)>=0} f(x)dx

is jointly continuous for y in R^r and u on the unit sphere, by dominated
convergence. Its minimum over the compact sphere is D_f(y), a continuous
function. The cap with normal y/|y| through y shows

    D_f(y)<=mu({|x|>=|y|}),

so D_f(y)->0 at infinity. At an interior positive point, every containing
halfspace contains at least half a sufficiently small ball on which f
has a positive lower bound; consequently D_f is positive there. Its
positive supremum is therefore attained on a compact ball. Any point
outside or on the boundary of the closed convex support has a separating
or supporting containing halfspace of zero measure. Thus a deepest point
y lies in its interior.

Let A={u:G(y,u)=alpha}; this is a nonempty compact subset of the sphere.
Suppose zero is outside conv(A). Strict separation gives a vector v and
delta>0 with u dot v>=delta for every u in A. The same lower bound with
delta/2 holds on a neighborhood N of A in the sphere. Moving y to
y-epsilon v strictly increases all caps with normals in N. More
precisely, take a ball around y on which f>=m>0. For small epsilon the
newly added slab has thickness at least epsilon delta/2 and contains
cross-sections of that ball of uniformly positive (r-1)-volume. Thus
G(y-epsilon v,u)>=alpha+c epsilon uniformly for u in N, with c>0.

On the compact complement of N the old masses exceed alpha by a uniform
positive amount. Joint continuity ensures they remain above alpha for
small epsilon. Hence D_f(y-epsilon v)>alpha, a contradiction. We have
zero in conv(A). Caratheodory's theorem selects at most r+1 vectors from
A and weights with the stated properties; discard any zero weights. QED.

## Lemma 4: radialization preserves the optimal depth value

Translate the deepest point y to zero. For a unit vector u define

    rho(u)^r=r integral_0^infinity t^(r-1)f(y+tu)dt,
    U={su:u is unit, 0<=s<=rho(u)}.

Then U is a convex body of volume one. For every closed halfspace H
whose boundary passes through zero,

    vol_r(U intersect H)=integral_{y+H} f.

Moreover zero is a maximum-depth point of the uniform distribution on U,
and its maximum depth equals alpha=max D_f.

Proof. Lemma 2 with p=r proves convexity; Lemma 1 supplies boundedness
and nonempty interior. Polar integration shows the halfspace identity,
because radial integration of the indicator of U yields rho(u)^r/r.
The same calculation over the whole sphere gives vol_r(U)=integral f=1.

The identity gives depth_U(0)=alpha. Choose the active normals from
Lemma 3. Their corresponding origin halfspaces each cut volume alpha
from U. For any w in R^r at least one u_i dot w is nonnegative, since
their positive weighted sum is zero. The halfspace

    {x:u_i dot x>=u_i dot w}

contains w and is contained in {x:u_i dot x>=0}. Its U-volume is at most
alpha. Hence depth_U(w)<=alpha for every w. This proves optimality at
zero and equality of the two maximum values. QED.

## Proof of the theorem

By Lemma 4, alpha is the maximum halfspace depth of a uniform convex
body U in the same dimension r. Apply ordinary Grunbaum's inequality
at the centroid of U to get alpha>=gamma_r. This proves the claim for
all r>=1. For r=1 it also follows immediately from the ordinary median
property. All halfspaces above are closed, and absolute continuity makes
their boundaries null without discarding any positive boundary mass.

## Sharpness and a larger equality family

Uniform measure on an r-simplex supplies sharpness. More generally let
T be a simplex with centroid zero, and let f(x)=c exp(-p_T(x)), where
p_T is the Minkowski gauge of T and c normalizes its integral. This is
a full-dimensional log-concave density. Its superlevel sets are positive
dilates of T. Layer-cake integration therefore gives exactly the same
fraction as uniform T for every halfspace through zero, so its depth
there is gamma_r. The affine permutations of the simplex vertices
preserve the density and average every point to zero. Since every depth
upper level set is convex (it is an intersection of halfspaces), this
symmetry implies that zero is deepest. Thus this nonuniform log-concave
family also attains equality.

## Background attribution and scope

Caplin--Nalebuff, *On 64%-Majority Rule* (1988), Theorem 2, uses
radialization at a maximum-depth point for ordinary concave densities.
Theorem 2.2 in Klartag's *On convex perturbations with a bounded isotropic
constant* states the non-even Ball theorem with only f(0)>0 and p>=1.
The quantile proof above supplies the precise convexity statement
directly, and all remaining steps have also been proved here.

Primary background links:

- https://faculty.econ.ucsb.edu/~tedb/Courses/UCSBpf/readings/NalebuffCaplan.pdf
- https://www.math.tau.ac.il/~klartagb/papers/perturb.pdf

No assertion about mixed-integer target construction follows merely
from this theorem. Such a construction remains a separate obligation.
